question: What is the primary function of sensory nerves in the peripheral nervous system?

options.A: Producing cerebrospinal fluid within the spinal ventricles
options.B: Carrying efferent signals from the brain to skeletal muscles
options.C: Transmitting afferent information from receptors to the central nervous system

explanation: Sensory nerves are classified as afferent fibers because their primary job is to convey sensory data inward toward the spinal cord and brain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h1)

question: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus develops a peripheral neuropathy affecting sensory nerves. What clinical outcome is most directly expected?

options.A: Inability to produce adequate cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Impaired perception of touch, temperature, and pain in the distal limbs
options.C: Hypersecretion of digestive enzymes in the gut
options.D: Complete paralysis of the lower extremities

explanation: Damage to peripheral sensory nerves disrupts the transmission of external stimuli like touch and pain, frequently manifesting as numbness or altered sensations in the hands and feet. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h1)

question: Where are the cell bodies of most sensory neurons residing outside the central nervous system primarily located?

options.B: Ventral horn of the spinal cord

explanation: The cell bodies of pseudo-unipolar sensory neurons aggregate in swellings along the dorsal roots of spinal nerves known as dorsal root ganglia. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h2)

question: How does fiber diameter and myelination affect the speed of action potential propagation in sensory neurons?

options.A: Thicker, heavily myelinated fibers conduct impulses more rapidly
options.B: Myelin sheath presence slows down conduction by blocking sodium channels
options.C: Thinner fibers with no myelin conduct impulses the fastest
options.D: Fiber structure has no impact on nerve conduction velocity

explanation: Larger cross-sectional area and the saltatory conduction provided by a myelin sheath greatly accelerate the speed at which nerve impulses travel along an axon. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h2)

question: Which category of sensory receptors is primarily responsible for detecting actual or potential tissue damage?
explanation: Nociceptors are specialized receptors that activate in response to noxious stimuli, translating physical or chemical trauma into pain signals. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h3)

question: A patient placing their hand on a hot iron quickly withdraws it due to activation of which receptor type?
explanation: Extreme heat stimulates both temperature-sensing thermoreceptors and pain-sensing nociceptors, prompting an immediate reflex withdrawal. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h3)

question: What local voltage change occurs in a sensory receptor membrane directly in response to an adequate stimulus?
explanation: The initial graded depolarization or hyperpolarization produced by a sensory stimulus at the receptor level is called a generator or receptor potential. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h4)

question: How does a sensory neuron encode a stronger physical stimulus intensity into electrical language?

options.A: By reversing the direction of axonal propagation
options.B: By decreasing the threshold required for activation
options.C: By increasing the amplitude of individual action potentials
options.D: By increasing the frequency of action potential firing

explanation: Because action potentials are all-or-none events with constant amplitude, stronger stimuli are encoded by firing action potentials at a higher frequency. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h4)

question: Which order of neuron in ascending sensory pathways typically crosses over (decussates) before reaching the thalamus?
explanation: Second-order neurons typically cross the midline within the spinal cord or brainstem before ascending to synapse in the thalamus. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h5)

question: A patient experiences a spinal cord lesion that interrupts the spinothalamic tract on the right side. Where will the resulting loss of pain and temperature sensation primarily manifest?

options.A: On the left side of the body
options.C: On the right side of the body

explanation: Because spinothalamic fibers cross the midline shortly after entering the spinal cord, a lesion on the right side affects sensory input originating from the contralateral (left) side of the body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h5)

question: In which specific region of the cerebral cortex is the primary somatosensory area located?

options.A: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
options.C: Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe

explanation: The primary somatosensory cortex is situated immediately behind the central sulcus, occupying the postcentral gyrus within the parietal lobe. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h6)

question: Why do the hands and face occupy a much larger portion of the sensory homunculus compared to the back or thigh?

options.A: They receive blood supply directly from the internal carotid artery system
options.B: They contain thick, heavily keratinized skin layers that accelerate signal transmission
options.C: They possess a much higher density of sensory receptors and require finer discrimination
options.D: They are located closer anatomically to the spinal cord entry points

explanation: Cortical representation size corresponds directly to receptor density and the need for detailed tactile discrimination rather than physical body size. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h6)

question: Which clinical test is commonly used to assess a patient's conscious proprioception and joint position sense?

options.A: Placing a vibrating tuning fork against the mastoid process
options.B: Scratching the sole of the foot with a blunt instrument
options.C: Shining a bright light directly into the pupil to check constriction
options.D: Moving a finger or toe up and down while the patient's eyes are closed

explanation: Joint position sense testing requires the patient to identify whether a digit has been moved upward or downward without visual cues. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h7)

question: During a routine sensory assessment, a nurse notices that a patient cannot feel light touch in a symmetrical 'glove-and-stocking' distribution across both hands and feet. What nursing conclusion is most appropriate?

options.A: This pattern indicates a complete transaction of the cervical spinal cord
options.B: The patient is likely demonstrating normal age-related sensory enhancement
options.C: The patient likely has a localized injury to a single cranial nerve
options.D: The findings suggest a systemic peripheral neuropathy commonly associated with metabolic conditions like diabetes

explanation: A symmetrical glove-and-stocking sensory loss pattern is the classic hallmark of distal symmetric polyneuropathy often seen in diabetes mellitus or nutritional deficiencies. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h7)
